ideas.name: long-travel geared prismatic jaw
ideas.description: The prismatic part's straight-sliding finger removes both failure mechanisms at once: the face never turns (0 deg at every width) and the tip never rises (+1 mm). The catalogue version tops out at 68 mm (60T pinion, 30 mm/rad x 1.92 rad), which would lose apple, banana and tomato can and cannot reach 73-96 mm. This design adds a 2:1 printed step-up stage: a 40T gear on the servo horn drives a 20T gear on a pinion shaft carrying a 44T module-1 pinion. Finger travel is 2 x 22 = 44 mm per servo rad, about 85 mm over the 1.92 rad range, giving fingertips from about 12 mm to about 100 mm apart. Squeeze is 1.62 / (2 x 0.022) = about 37 N, more than the stock 20 N. The carriage rides two 150 mm rods instead of 100 mm so the full travel fits.
ideas.test: Add a prismatic jaw variant to the simulator with a gear_ratio parameter (2.0) and rod length 150 mm, so travel is 44 mm per servo rad with the 44T pinion. Re-run all 21 objects, especially dice (17 mm, needing about 0.1 rad resolution) and mustard (96 mm, near full travel).

ideas.name: twin-rack symmetric parallel gripper
ideas.description: One printed 60T module-1 pinion on the gripper servo horn drives two opposed racks. Each rack is printed on a carriage that runs on two LM3UU bushings over two shared 3 x 150 mm ground steel rods, and each carriage carries one jaw finger with the existing TPU pads. The jaws close symmetrically about the pinion, so the opening changes by 60 mm per servo radian (about 115 mm over the 1.92 rad servo range). The faces never turn and the tips never rise. The squeeze per jaw is the servo torque over twice the pitch radius, about 27 N at 7.4 V.
ideas.test: A jaw builder in the simulator with two prismatic joints coupled by a gear constraint (opposite sign, 30 mm per servo rad each), on a rod frame 150 mm long, plus the pad geometry on both fingers. Then re-run all 21 objects, so System 1 can re-tune side clearance for a centred grasp.

ideas.name: self-aligning swivel pad on the stock revolute jaw
ideas.description: The moving jaw's rigid tilted pad is replaced by a printed pad carrier that pivots on an M3 shoulder screw running in two MR63 bearings pressed into a printed clevis at the stock fingertip. The pivot axis is horizontal and runs across the jaw width. The carrier holds a 12 mm wide, 3 mm thick face (2 mm PLA plus a 1 mm TPU skin, friction 0.9) that extends 12 mm below the pivot and 8 mm above it. A printed TPU bumper on each side of the clevis centres the carrier at the old 17 deg pad angle and lets it swing ±45 deg. On contact, the face rotates until it lies flat on the object's side wall, so the contact normal is horizontal at every opening and the face's corner cannot catch the object's top edge. The fixed jaw gets a rigid pad of the same face thickness with 12 mm reach, so both pad bottoms are level when the jaw is closed. Thinner faces raise the widest opening from 91 to about 95 mm, and squeeze stays about 20 N because the lever is still about 81 mm.
ideas.test: The simulator needs a passive hinged pad body on the moving jaw: a revolute joint at the fingertip with an axis across the jaw width, a stiff torsional spring and damper modelling the TPU bumper centred at 17 deg, ±45 deg limits, and a 3 mm face with friction 0.9 hanging 12 mm below the pivot. It also needs a fixed-jaw pad with reach 12. Run all 21 groups, with tuna, pudding and sugar the target gains.

ideas.name: full-width sector-gear prismatic jaw (manifest-only)
ideas.description: The stock moving jaw is replaced by a printed carriage. It rides two LM3UU bushings on two 3x100 mm steel rods clamped in a printed frame on the gripper body, parallel to the closing axis, with the rods' full length used for travel. The carriage carries the moving finger, which has its own straight rack along the outer edge. A printed module-1 sector gear with a ~47 mm pitch radius (only ~115 deg of teeth, so it stays compact) is bolted to the gripper servo horn and drives that rack. The finger travels about 47 mm per servo radian, ~90 mm over the -0.17..1.75 rad span, for an opening of about 12-102 mm. The finger neither turns nor rises, and its face stays vertical at every opening. The existing pads move over with pad_angle set to 0, since on a slide any pad tilt becomes a constant face tilt; TPU stays at 2 mm, groove/lip/reach at 0. A vertical flat face touches a sphere exactly at its equator, so the held round objects stay antipodally gripped.
ideas.test: A jaw builder for a prismatic finger whose travel per radian (pitch radius) is decoupled from pinion diameter by a sector gear, with travel limited by rod length (90 mm usable on 100 mm rods). In effect, the existing prismatic type with pinion radius extended to ~47 mm and an opening cap of ~102 mm. Run it with pads at pad_angle 0 against all 21 groups, especially tuna, pudding, sugar and mustard, and the small objects (dice, marker, cube), to check squeeze stays under the force limit.

ideas.name: long-stroke printed-dovetail rack-and-pinion parallel jaw
ideas.description: This replaces the hinged moving jaw. A 140 mm PLA dovetail rail is bolted to the gripper body along the closing axis, and the moving finger is printed in one piece with a dovetail carriage and a module-1 rack 110 mm long. A 50T module-1 PLA pinion (pitch radius 25 mm) is screwed to the STS3215 horn and meshes with the rack, so the finger travels 25 mm per servo radian. Over about 3.6 rad of servo travel the fingertips go from about 15 to 105 mm apart. The finger slides straight, so its face stays parallel to the fixed face and its tip stays level with the fixed tip at every opening. That removes both the R(1-cos q) rise and the 45 deg tilt that put the moving pad on the top face of the 85-96 mm low objects. A printed preload gib with M3 set screws takes up dovetail clearance. The existing pads module mounts on the carriage face at pad_angle 0.
ideas.test: Simulator builder: a prismatic jaw variant whose travel is not limited by the 100 mm rod. Settings: rail length 140 mm, pinion_teeth 50, servo range -0.17..3.6 rad (opening about 15-105 mm), slide friction about 0.3 (PLA on PLA), tip offset +0 mm, face 0 deg with pads at pad_angle 0 and groove_mm about 2. Run all 21 groups, with System 1 also tuning a gripper torque limit.

ideas.name: centred-sweep parallelogram jaw (phase-offset four-bar)
ideas.description: Two printed PLA links, each 90 mm between pivots, carry the moving finger as a parallelogram four-bar, so the finger face stays vertical, parallel to the fixed jaw, at every opening. The driving link is keyed to the gripper-servo horn at a 0.31 rad offset, and the mount's pivot sits further out. Together these make the links vertical (fingertip lowest) at a 45 mm opening rather than at closed. The finger then sweeps about ±35° around that lowest point. The tip stays within about +4 mm of the fixed tip for 17 to 75 mm objects, +9 to +13 mm at 85 to 92 mm, and about +16 mm at 96 mm. It opens past 100 mm, and the horn sweep is under 1 rad. Pivots run on four MR63 bearings with M3 shafts. The existing TPU pads mount on the finger at pad_angle 0 (vertical face). About 20 g of PLA is added at the wrist, roughly 0.03 N*m at the shoulder.
ideas.test: Add a link-phase parameter to the simulator's parallelogram jaw: the fingertip opening at which the links are vertical (here 45 mm), with link_mm = 90. Pads go to pad_angle_deg = 0, keeping pad_tpu_mm = 2, reach 0, groove 0, lip 0. Then rerun all 21 objects, checking two things: that the links do not collide with small objects at the closed end (the iteration-2 force_limit at t = 0.02 s on the wood cube), and the tip height against each object's top or equator.

ideas.name: scissor (lazy-tongs) straight-line moving jaw
ideas.description:
A single-stage printed scissor linkage (two 60 mm PLA link pairs crossed at their middles) replaces the hinged moving jaw. At the servo end, one link end is pinned to the gripper servo horn and the other slides in a printed slot. At the output end, one link end is pinned to a finger carriage plate and the other slides in a slot on that plate, so the plate translates along the closing axis without turning or rising.

The finger opening is x = 120 cos(theta). Over theta 82 to 37 deg (0.79 rad of servo travel, inside the stock window) the opening runs 15 to 96 mm, with squeeze tau/(0.12 sin theta), about 14-20 N. The TPU pad mounts on the carriage at pad_angle 0, so its face is parallel to the fixed jaw at every opening and its tip stays a few mm above the table for every object width. The fixed jaw is unchanged.
ideas.test: A jaw builder for a scissor finger: a prismatic joint along the closing axis with a nonlinear transmission from the servo angle q (x = 2nL cos(theta0 - q), force = tau / (2nL sin theta)). Parameters: link_mm [40, 70] and stages n in {1, 2}. Face orientation is fixed at 0 deg and fingertip height is constant. Add slot-pin compliance of about 0.3 mm as a small rotational play on the carriage. Then rerun all 21 groups with System 1 re-tuning the grasp.

ideas.name: TPU living-hinge self-aligning pad (manifest-only)
ideas.description: A PLA pad plate is joined to a PLA base screwed onto the moving jaw by a 1.2 mm TPU flexure strip at the pad's lower third. The flexure axis is horizontal, along the jaw width. Its rest angle is 20 deg and it can rotate passively by about ±35 deg, with soft centring stiffness. When the pad meets an object's side, the contact moments about the flexure even out and turn the plate flat against the side, so the normal stays horizontal and opposed to the fixed jaw at any opening from 17 to 91 mm. Because the pivot is low, the plate's bottom swings in at wide openings and meets the side below the top.
ideas.test: The simulator would need a pads variant whose moving face is a separate body on a hinge joint (spring stiffness about 0.05 N*m/rad, damping, limits ±35 deg) at a set height above the fingertip. It should be run on all 21 objects, with tuna, pudding and sugar as the targets and potted_meat_can and dice as the guard cases.

ideas.name: twin-rack symmetric parallel gripper on stacked 3x100 rod pairs (manifest-only)
ideas.description: A printed 60T module-1 pinion sits on the gripper servo horn. Two printed racks mesh with it at the top and bottom, so they move in opposite directions. Each rack belongs to a carriage that carries one jaw (the fixed jaw becomes a second moving jaw). Each carriage rides its own pair of 3x100 mm ground steel rods on two LM3UU bushings. The two rod pairs are stacked vertically in a printed housing, so the carriages pass each other without collision and each gets 58 mm of travel. Both fingers stay vertical and at constant height. The opening runs 0 to about 115 mm, at 27 N per jaw. The existing printed TPU pads mount on the carriage fingers with M2 screws.
ideas.test: A builder for a 'twin_prismatic' jaw: two slide joints coupled at a 1:-1 gear ratio to the gripper servo through a pinion of radius teeth/2 mm, with fingers that keep their orientation, a range of 0 to 58 mm per side, and squeeze = torque/(2r). Run all 21 objects, with System 1 refitting side clearance and the close target.

ideas.name: opening-compensated telescoping pad on the revolute jaw
ideas.description: The moving pad sits on a printed dovetail slider along the moving jaw. A printed push-link from a pivot on the gripper body to the slider (MR63 bearings at both ends) pushes the pad down the jaw as the hinge opens, by about 81(1-cos(q-0.6)) mm above 0.6 rad. This keeps the fingertip level with the fixed one at wide openings and adds opening at the tip. The TPU skin is kept.
ideas.test: A pad builder whose reach_mm is a function of jaw angle: reach(q) = max(0, 81(1 - cos(q - 0.6))), applied to the moving pad only. Run all 21 objects.

ideas.name: compound-geared long-stroke prismatic jaw (3x100 rods, 48T:16T + 28T pinion)
ideas.description: The moving finger rides a carriage with one LM3UU bushing on each of two parallel 3x100 mm steel rods, so it slides straight along the closing axis without turning or rising. The servo horn carries a printed 48T module-1 gear. It drives a 16T gear on an idler shaft (an M3 screw in two MR63 bearings), and a 28T pinion on the same shaft drives a printed rack on the carriage. That gives 42 mm of finger travel per servo radian and a 16 to 98 mm gap over the -0.17..1.75 rad range. Squeeze is about 30 N, constant at every opening. Every gear stays 50 mm across or less, so the gripper stays compact; a direct 86T pinion would be 88 mm across.
ideas.test: Add a prismatic-jaw variant to the simulator with a gear ratio parameter: effective radius = pinion_r * driver_r / driven_r, here 14*24/8 = 42 mm. Use the 82 mm stroke limit and a closed gap of 14 mm. Then run all 21 groups with pads pad_angle 0, TPU 2 mm.

proposals.edit: pads -> pads (groove_mm=2, lip_mm=1, pad_angle_deg=20, pad_tpu_mm=2, reach_mm=15, width_mm=20)
proposals.mechanism: slipped_under_load (potted_meat_can: rose 28 of 30 mm and slid, metal mu 0.35 on bare PLA 0.45) and squeezed_down_out (rva000_gelatin_box: moving face 33 deg off vertical, pushing down, bare PLA cannot resist)
proposals.principle: A tilted contact squeezes the object out when N sin(a) beats the friction mu N cos(a), so it holds only while tan(a) < mu. A TPU skin raises mu from 0.45 to 0.9, which puts the self-locking limit at about 42 deg instead of 24 deg. Friction capacity 2 mu N also doubles against the 370 g can. Tilting the pad back 20 deg moves the parallel opening to about 0.35 rad (about 45 mm).
proposals.hypothesis: Pads change the face angle by about (stock + 6 - pad_angle): the brief gives +20 deg at 35 mm for angle 0 against +14 stock, and -21 deg for angle 45. With pad_angle 20 the faces become about -13 deg on dice and markers, about 0 deg at 35 mm, about +14 deg at 55 mm, about +28 deg at gelatin's 73 mm and about +30 deg at apple's 75 mm (+44 on stock). With mu 0.9, every one of those is under the about 42 deg self-locking limit. Potted meat (59 mm, about +17 deg) gains double friction, so it should stop slipping in the last 2 mm. Gelatin rva000 had only 33 deg of tilt and was squeezed out. At about 28 deg with TPU it should lock, and the moving tip sits about +8 mm against a 30 mm tall box. This is the cheapest move ($0, 0 days, about 30 machine min). No params-only move exists, because the current body has no tunable parameters.
risks: dice / large_marker / wood_block_cube: the face turns about 13 deg bottom-in and the moving tip sits about 4 mm below the fixed one, which pushes the object up slightly. TPU mu 0.9 against tan13 = 0.23 leaves a large margin, and 13 mm of overlap remains on the 17 mm dice.
apple / banana / tomato_soup_can: the maximum opening drops from 99 to about 93 mm, still well above 75 mm. Their faces become less tilted than today.
golf_ball / round fruit: the 2 mm groove and the less-tilted face should centre them better, not worse.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face: on the wide, low boxes the hinged face is 44-60 deg off vertical with the bottom swung out, and the tip is +11 to +17 mm, so the moving jaw lands on the top edge (contacts pushing 67-86 deg down) and the fixed jaw often never touches (fixed_jaw_missed).
proposals.principle: A face that turns with its joint is parallel at only one opening. The pad tilt chooses that opening, so a steeper pad moves it toward the wide objects. The brief shows that at pad_angle 45 the tip at 85 mm drops from +23 to +14 and the face from +53 to +14 deg. TPU raises the tolerable tilt to about 42 deg.
proposals.hypothesis: At pad_angle 32 the estimated face is: gelatin 73 mm about +22 deg with tip about +8 against 30 mm tall; tuna 85 mm about +33 deg with tip about +18 against 34 mm; pudding 90 mm about +38 deg with tip about +22 against 38 mm. All of these are under the 42 deg TPU limit and below the tops, so both jaws reach the sides instead of the top edge. Small objects get about -25 deg bottom-in (tan25 = 0.47 < 0.9). This is the more aggressive point on the same part. If it breaks a small object, the loop's 4 fitting trials can search pad_angle between 20 and 32. Sugar box (92 mm) is marginal against a maximum opening of about 94 mm, and mustard (96 mm) is out of reach with any pad, so I do not claim either.
risks: dice / large_marker / wood_block_cube: the face turns about 25 deg bottom-in and the moving tip goes about 7 mm below the fixed one, which costs about 7 mm of overlap on the 17 mm dice. This is the main risk. TPU friction is what should save it.
screwdriver (34 mm, 35 tall): tilt about -6 deg, probably fine.
Round held objects: the parallel point moves to about 0.56 rad (about 60 mm), which is near lemon, cup and racquetball. The groove helps, so these are probably improved.
proposals.result: refused before trial: mechanism law (no interference): the fixed pad and the moving pad share material, a region up to 4.7 x 19.9 x 2.0 mm (jaw at 0.07 rad); parts may share material only at a bearing seat, within 10 mm of the hinge axis

iterations.notes:
I'm proposing two pad swaps and one design idea. The current body has no tunable parameters, so a parameter-only change wasn't possible.

**What's failing.** Two separate problems:
- **Potted meat can and gelatin box (rva000):** these slip or get squeezed out because bare PLA is too slippery (friction 0.45). On a face tilted more than about 24 deg, the object gets pushed out.
- **The five wide, low boxes and cans (73–96 mm across, 30–58 mm tall):** on the hinged jaw, the face tilts 44–64 deg at those widths and the moving fingertip rises 11–35 mm. So the moving jaw lands on the box's top edge, and in two runs the fixed jaw never touched the object.

**Proposals 1 and 2 (pads):**
- Both add a TPU skin, which raises friction from 0.45 to 0.9. A tilted face then holds up to about 42 deg instead of about 24 deg.
- Both tilt the pad back so its face is parallel at a wider opening: 20 deg in proposal 1 (safer for small objects), 32 deg in proposal 2 (aimed at the boxes).
- Each costs $0 and about 30 machine minutes, using printer time and screws on hand.
- They're both in the pads slot, so they won't be tried together.
- The main risk is the small objects (dice, marker, wood cube). Their faces would tilt 13–25 deg bottom-in, and I'm counting on the TPU friction to hold them.

**What the pads can't fix.**
- **Mustard bottle (96 mm):** pads cut the maximum opening from 99 mm to 92–95 mm, so it's out of reach.
- **Sugar box (92 mm):** borderline, so I'm not predicting it.

**Proposal 3 (idea, not testable here).** No catalogue jaw covers 17–96 mm with vertical faces:
- The 90 mm parallelogram's fingertip rises 33 mm at 85 mm.
- The prismatic jaw stops at 68 mm, which would lose the apple, banana and soup can.

So I'm recording a sliding jaw with a 2:1 gear step-up and longer rods:
- **Reach and grip:** fingertips about 12–100 mm apart, about 37 N squeeze.
- **Cost:** about $9.20, 3 days lead time and about 200 machine minutes.
- **Parts to buy:** 2 linear bushings and 2 pivot bearings from the manifest, plus 3 × 150 mm steel rods, which aren't on the manifest. I've guessed $2.50 each with 3 days lead time.

**Budget.** The 12 V servo swap still isn't needed. At 1.18 N·m, holding the heaviest object (514 g) needs less than the 1.62 N·m stall torque, and the swap costs $68 against $40 left.

iterations.notes:
I'm proposing two body changes this round; the trial decides what's kept.

1. **Parallelogram jaw, 90 mm links** (costs $3.60 for four bearings, 3 days, 82 machine minutes). The wide boxes fail because the stock moving face tilts 44–64 degrees at 75–95 mm openings. Its upper part hits the box's top edge and presses down instead of squeezing. The parallelogram keeps the face vertical at every opening. I expect it to pick up the gelatin box and the potted meat can, with the tuna can marginal.

2. **Friction-only pads** (free, about 16 machine minutes). A rubber-like (TPU) skin doubles grip from 0.45 to 0.9, with the pad angled about 7 degrees so the jaw shape stays close to stock. This targets the potted meat can, which slipped while gripped only 4 mm below its top. It also tests whether the 8 groups lost in iteration 1 came from the pads themselves or from their 15 mm reach and 20-degree angle.

**What neither change fixes: tip rise.** Even with a vertical face, the moving fingertip ends up too high on the widest objects:
- Tuna can (85 mm wide, 34 tall): the tip rises about 33 mm against a 34 mm top, so it's marginal.
- Pudding box (90 mm, 38 tall) and sugar box (92 mm, 45 tall): the tip probably rises past or close to their tops.
- Mustard bottle (96 mm): the tip lands above its middle, so it would be pushed down.

These need a finger that slides straight in without rising. The 60-tooth prismatic jaw in the catalogue does that but only opens to 68 mm, which would lose the apple and banana. The long-travel geared prismatic jaw recorded in iteration 1 is the real fix. It needs 3×150 mm steel rods, which aren't on the manifest; I estimate $5, and it fits the budget. The 12 V servos aren't the issue here, and they're out of budget anyway ($68 against $40 left).

Each rack sits on a carriage that carries one jaw, and the two carriages slide on two shared 3 x 150 mm steel rods. idea.name: twin-rack symmetric parallel gripper
idea.description: One printed 60T module-1 pinion on the gripper servo horn drives two opposed racks. Each rack is printed on a carriage that runs on two LM3UU bushings over two shared 3 x 150 mm ground steel rods, and each carriage carries one jaw finger with the existing TPU pads. The jaws close symmetrically about the pinion, so the opening changes by 60 mm per servo radian (about 115 mm over the 1.92 rad servo range). The faces never turn and the tips never rise. The squeeze per jaw is the servo torque over twice the pitch radius, about 27 N at 7.4 V.
idea.test: A jaw builder in the simulator with two prismatic joints coupled by a gear constraint (opposite sign, 30 mm per servo rad each), on a rod frame 150 mm long, plus the pad geometry on both fingers. Then re-run all 21 objects, so System 1 can re-tune side clearance for a centred grasp.

iterations.notes:
I made two proposals: a cheap pad setting aimed at the gelatin box, and a new jaw idea for the wide objects.

**Diagnosis.** There are two separate problems.
1. **Gelatin box (73 mm wide, 30 mm tall): the moving face is too tilted.** At that opening the face is 44 deg off parallel. The tip is below the top, but the face presses the box down and squeezes it out. It nearly passed: it rose 29 mm and ended at +26 mm.
2. **Pudding box, sugar box, mustard bottle and tuna can: the jaw doesn't open wide enough.** The jaw opens to 91 mm at most (95 mm at pad_angle 45), and the tip rises 19 to 29 mm near full opening. So the moving jaw lands on the top face. Sugar (92 mm) and mustard (96 mm) are wider than the jaw opens at all.

**What the catalogue can't do:**
- **Parallelogram jaw:** the face stays upright, but the tip rises 48 mm at 85 mm, far above the tuna can's 34 mm top. It already lost 7 held groups when tried.
- **Prismatic jaw:** it opens 58 mm at most, so it would drop apple, banana, tennis ball and tomato soup can.
- **12 V servos:** refused on cost ($68 against $40 left). The arm doesn't need them anyway: the heaviest object is 514 g, which needs about 1.18 N*m at the shoulder against a 1.62 N*m stall.

**Proposal 1 (pads, pad_angle 7 → 17, nothing else changed).** This sits between two settings already tried:
- pad_angle 7 held all 16 groups.
- pad_angle 30 held all but the potted meat can, though it gained nothing.

Expected effect on gelatin: the face goes from about 44 to about 34 deg, and the tip stays about 15 mm below the 30 mm top.

The risk is the potted meat can, which is metal with friction 0.35. At 17 its face is about +19 deg, closer to the setting that held it (7) than the one that lost it (30). The dice, marker and cube all held at 30, so they should hold here.

I'm not confident about the gelatin gain: pad_angle 30 should have flattened its face even more and still didn't gain it. The record doesn't say why.

**Proposal 2 (idea, not tested): a twin-rack symmetric parallel gripper.** It differs from the long-travel prismatic jaw recorded in iteration 1:
- **How it works:** both jaws ride on one pinion, so the stroke doubles without going beyond the 60-tooth limit. That gives about 115 mm of travel with vertical faces and level tips.
- **Grip:** about 27 N per jaw.
- **Cost:** about $9.80 (4 LM3UU bearings at $1.20, plus about $5 for two 3 × 150 mm rods, which aren't on the manifest), 3 days lead time, about 200 machine minutes.

It's the only body I see that could take all four wide objects plus gelatin. It would need re-tuning for every held group, because the fixed jaw would move too.

On each, the moving jaw's contact sits at or just under the top (tuna +16 vs top +17, pudding +18 vs +19, sugar +22 vs +23, mustard +29 vs +29) and pushes 83 to 88 deg down. In the brief's numbers, at 85 mm the rigid revolute pad face is 45 deg off parallel with its bottom swung out, and the moving fingertip is +29 mm. The widest opening is 91 mm, which leaves 1 mm around pudding and none around sugar or mustard.
proposals.principle: Two contacts hold only when their normals are horizontal and opposed. A face that turns with its joint is parallel at one opening only. A face that pivots freely and lies flat against the object's vertical side has a horizontal normal at every opening, so no N sin(a) squeezes the object out and the corner of the face cannot catch the top rim. The fingertip on a swinging joint still rises by about R(1 - cos q). A pad that hangs below its pivot puts the contact patch on the side wall, below the object's top.
proposals.hypothesis: No catalogue part covers both the heavy mid-size cans and the wide boxes. On the revolute, pad_angle shifts the single parallel opening. Raising it from 7 to 17 gained gelatin, but 30 lost potted_meat_can (slipped_under_load). Tuna (metal, mu 0.35) needs its face within about 19 deg at 85 mm, which means pad_angle near 45 or more, and that would drop the 35 to 57 mm groups. The parallelogram keeps a constant face but its tip rises +49 mm at 85 mm, above every failing object's top, and in iteration 2 it lost 7 groups. The prismatic opens to at most 58 mm, which would lose apple, banana, gelatin, tennis and tomato. The 12 V servos are refused on budget and do not address this mechanism anyway. The proposed part keeps the stock hinge and gives the moving jaw a self-aligning pad. A pad carrier turns on an M3 shaft held in two MR63 bearings at the jaw tip, on an axis across the jaw width. It is centred by a TPU bumper with about ±45 deg of compliance. Its 3 mm face (2 mm PLA plus 1 mm TPU), 12 mm wide, hangs 12 mm below the pivot. The fixed pad gets a matching 12 mm reach, so both bottoms are level at small openings. For tuna at about 0.8 rad, the pivot sits about +16 mm on the 34 mm can, so the flat patch covers roughly +4 to +16 mm on the vertical wall with a horizontal normal. Pudding (38 tall) and sugar (45 tall) work the same way, with more room under the top. Faces are about 2 mm thinner per side than the current 5 mm pads, and the bare jaw opens to 99 mm, so the widest opening rises from 91 to roughly 95 mm. That clears pudding (90) and sugar (92). Mustard at 96 mm stays out of reach, so I do not claim it. Squeeze stays about 20 N. Sugar: 2 x 0.5 x 20 = 20 N against 5.0 N of weight, and the shoulder needs 0.41 + 0.77 = 1.18 N*m, under the 1.62 stall. Tuna: 2 x 0.35 x 21 = 14.7 N against 1.7 N.

rolling objects (golf_ball, plum, strawberry, lemon, racquetball, tennis_ball, apple): a free flat pad sets its contact normal along the line from the pivot to the sphere centre. If the pivot is above the equator, the normal tilts down by a few degrees, which TPU friction (0.9 on the pad, 0.4 to 0.9 on the objects) should hold. The groove option is lost on the moving side.

dice and large_marker (17 to 19 mm, 17 to 19 tall): the 12 mm hanging pads have to clear each other and the table when nearly closed. In iteration 1, reach 15 together with pad_angle 20 and width 20 lost 8 groups, so this reach is kept to 12 mm with width 12 and no lip, and the fixed and moving bottoms are levelled at closure.

idea.name: self-aligning swivel pad on the stock revolute jaw
idea.description: The moving jaw's rigid tilted pad is replaced by a printed pad carrier that pivots on an M3 shoulder screw running in two MR63 bearings pressed into a printed clevis at the stock fingertip. The pivot axis is horizontal and runs across the jaw width. The carrier holds a 12 mm wide, 3 mm thick face (2 mm PLA plus a 1 mm TPU skin, friction 0.9) that extends 12 mm below the pivot and 8 mm above it. A printed TPU bumper on each side of the clevis centres the carrier at the old 17 deg pad angle and lets it swing ±45 deg. On contact, the face rotates until it lies flat on the object's side wall, so the contact normal is horizontal at every opening and the face's corner cannot catch the object's top edge. The fixed jaw gets a rigid pad of the same face thickness with 12 mm reach, so both pad bottoms are level when the jaw is closed. Thinner faces raise the widest opening from 91 to about 95 mm, and squeeze stays about 20 N because the lever is still about 81 mm.
idea.test: The simulator needs a passive hinged pad body on the moving jaw: a revolute joint at the fingertip with an axis across the jaw width, a stiff torsional spring and damper modelling the TPU bumper centred at 17 deg, ±45 deg limits, and a 3 mm face with friction 0.9 hanging 12 mm below the pivot. It also needs a fixed-jaw pad with reach 12. Run all 21 groups, with tuna, pudding and sugar the target gains.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face. In all 8 failing tasks the moving jaw lands on the object's top face, pushing 83-88 deg down, and the fixed jaw gets little or no contact. The cause is the revolute jaw's kinematics at wide openings. The brief says the fingertips open at most 91 mm. At 85 mm the moving face is 45 deg off parallel with the bottom swung out, so the jaw above the tip leans inward, and the tip has risen +29 mm. The objects are 85-96 mm across, and some are low: tuna 34 mm tall, pudding 38 mm. With side clearance the jaw cannot pass beside them, so it comes down on the top edge (contacts at +16..+29 mm against tops at +17..+29).
proposals.principle: A finger can hold an object's side only if, at that object's opening, the fingertip reaches below the object's top with clearance above the table. The two faces must also be antipodal (normals horizontal and opposed). A finger that slides straight along the closing axis neither turns nor rises, so both conditions hold at every opening. The opening is then set only by the slide's travel: pitch radius times servo range.
proposals.hypothesis: The catalogue has nothing that covers 85-96 mm. On the revolute the opening is capped at 91-95 mm by the 1.20 rad hinge stop. Pad parameters are used up: pad_angle 30 gained none of the four objects and lost potted_meat_can, and the reach-15 pads lost 8-10 groups. The parallelogram at link 90 tops out at 96 mm with the tip at +49 mm at 85 mm, and its trial lost 7 groups. The catalogue prismatic tops out at 58 mm at 60T. 12 V servos are refused on budget ($68 vs $40), and torque is not the problem anyway: sugar needs 0.41+0.77=1.18 N*m against 1.62. The two earlier rack ideas need 3x150 rods, which the manifest does not provide, so they cannot be built. This design stays inside the manifest. The two 3x100 rods allow about 90 mm of carriage travel. A printed sector gear with a ~47 mm pitch radius covers that 90 mm over the servo's ~1.92 rad span. That gives an opening of about 12-102 mm, so dice at 17 mm and the 92 mm sugar box both fit. Squeeze is 1.62/0.047 ≈ 34 N at stall, and System 1 can still lower it with the close target. The holding check is 2·mu·N = 2·0.9·20 ≈ 36 N with TPU, against 5 N for the 514 g sugar box. With the faces vertical and no tip rise, the pads touch the box sides at table clearance, below the 34-45 mm tops. Mustard (96 mm) is marginal at ~3 mm clearance per side.
risks: dice, large_marker, wood_block_cube: the squeeze at small openings rises to ~34 N stall. The parallelogram lost the cube and the foam brick to force_limit. Here squeeze is constant (torque/radius), not rising near closure as it does on a linkage, and System 1 controls the close target.

golf_ball, apple, tennis_ball, lemon, plum, strawberry, racquetball (rolling): today they are held with slightly tilted faces. Vertical faces touch spheres at the equator, which is antipodal, but nothing centres them along the pad. If they slip sideways, groove_mm would be the fix.
potted_meat_can, tomato_soup_can (heavy metal): they rely on the TPU friction, which is kept. At ~20 N squeeze, 2·0.9·20=36 N against 3.6 N weight.
foam_brick: it previously failed on force_limit under higher squeeze. The close target must stay soft.

idea.name: full-width sector-gear prismatic jaw (manifest-only)
idea.description: The stock moving jaw is replaced by a printed carriage. It rides two LM3UU bushings on two 3x100 mm steel rods clamped in a printed frame on the gripper body, parallel to the closing axis, with the rods' full length used for travel. The carriage carries the moving finger, which has its own straight rack along the outer edge. A printed module-1 sector gear with a ~47 mm pitch radius (only ~115 deg of teeth, so it stays compact) is bolted to the gripper servo horn and drives that rack. The finger travels about 47 mm per servo radian, ~90 mm over the -0.17..1.75 rad span, for an opening of about 12-102 mm. The finger neither turns nor rises, and its face stays vertical at every opening. The existing pads move over with pad_angle set to 0, since on a slide any pad tilt becomes a constant face tilt; TPU stays at 2 mm, groove/lip/reach at 0. A vertical flat face touches a sphere exactly at its equator, so the held round objects stay antipodally gripped.
idea.test: A jaw builder for a prismatic finger whose travel per radian (pitch radius) is decoupled from pinion diameter by a sector gear, with travel limited by rod length (90 mm usable on 100 mm rods). In effect, the existing prismatic type with pinion radius extended to ~47 mm and an opening cap of ~102 mm. Run it with pads at pad_angle 0 against all 21 groups, especially tuna, pudding, sugar and mustard, and the small objects (dice, marker, cube), to check squeeze stays under the force limit.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face. This failure appears in all four failing groups: tuna 85 mm, pudding 90 mm, sugar 92 mm and mustard 96 mm. On the stock hinge the moving fingertip rises R(1-cos q) as the jaw opens. The brief gives +29 mm at 85 mm, and the measured rise is +13 to +18 mm at closing. The moving face also tilts 45 deg bottom-out at 85 mm, and the opening is capped at 91 mm by the 1.20 rad stop. So on approach the moving pad sits above or over the top edge. Every trace shows it pressing 83-88 deg down on the top at +16 to +29 mm, against tops at +17 to +29, while the fixed jaw has no contact or only 4-10 N.
proposals.principle: Two contacts hold only when their normals are horizontal and opposed, and only when the fingertip reaches below the object's top. A finger that slides straight along the closing axis neither turns nor rises (no R(1-cos q) term). Its face stays parallel to the fixed face at every opening, and its tip stays level with the fixed tip. Squeeze is servo torque over the pinion radius. The catalogue prismatic is capped at 58 mm only because its carriage rides on 3 x 100 mm rods. The principle itself does not cap it.
proposals.hypothesis:
No catalogue part or parameter can address this, and the numbers show it.
(1) Pads params: 4 trials gained one group. pad_angle 30 lost potted_meat_can (57 mm, slipped_under_load), and 0.5 mm TPU at 17 or 22 deg lost it too (squeezed_down_out). Tuna (metal, mu 0.35) needs its face within about 19 deg at 85 mm, which takes pad_angle near 40. The hinge has a single parallel opening, so it cannot serve 57 mm and 85-96 mm at once. Pad params also cannot lift the 91-95 mm cap above sugar's 92 or mustard's 96.
(2) Parallelogram swap at link 90: tip +49 mm at 85 mm, above tuna's 34 mm and pudding's 38 mm tops. It already lost 7 groups in iteration 2. At link 50 it caps at 56 mm.
(3) Prismatic swap: 58 mm maximum even at 60T, so it loses apple, banana, tennis, gelatin and soup can.
(4) 12 V servos are refused on budget ($68 against $40), and they address arm torque, which is not the mechanism.
Earlier prismatic ideas depended on 3 x 150 rods that are not on the manifest. This one replaces the rods with a printed PLA dovetail rail 140 mm long, so it uses manifest items only and costs $0. A 50T module-1 pinion on the servo horn (pitch radius 25 mm, 52 mm across) drives a printed rack on the carriage. The STS3215 is a 360 deg position servo, so if the stops allow about 3.6 rad, the travel is 25 x 3.6 = 90 mm and the fingertips run from about 15 mm to about 105 mm apart. That covers dice (17 mm) through mustard (96 mm) with clearance. Tip offset stays about +0 to +2 mm (the catalogue prismatic shows +2 mm at both 35 and 55 mm), well below every failing top (17-29 mm above centre). Pads would go to pad_angle 0 so both faces are vertical.
Squeeze: 1.62 N*m / 0.025 m = 65 N at stall, less dovetail friction. The servo's torque-limit register (a control setting) would cap it near 20-30 N. The heaviest case is sugar at 514 g with mu 0.5: it needs 2 x 0.5 x N >= 5.0 N x 1.5, so N >= 7.6 N. Mustard (mu 0.4) needs about 8 N. Both are well covered.
Arm load: about 50 g printed parts replace the stock jaw. Plus 514 g of sugar, the shoulder needs 0.41 + 0.77 + about 0.08 = about 1.26 N*m, under the 1.62 N*m stall.
risks: Round objects (apple, golf_ball, lemon, plum, racquetball, strawberry, tennis_ball, tomato_soup_can) now ride on tilted hinge faces. With parallel vertical faces they are held only by friction at the equator. Mitigation: pads groove_mm of about 2 centres them, and the faces are exactly antipodal, so there is no N sin(a) ejection.
foam_brick and the other light objects could hit force_limit, since stall squeeze is 65 N against 20 N now. This survives only if the servo torque limit is set to about 30%.
potted_meat_can (370 g, mu 0.35) needs N >= about 8 N with vertical faces. That is easily met, and the vertical face removes the squeezed_down_out mechanism that lost it at pad_angle 22-30.
Small objects (dice 17 mm, large_marker 19 mm) need the carriage to close to below 17 mm. The rack must extend far enough that the minimum opening is no more than about 12 mm.
The printed dovetail carries more slop and friction than rods. Wobble could tilt the face by a degree or two.

idea.name: long-stroke printed-dovetail rack-and-pinion parallel jaw
idea.description: This replaces the hinged moving jaw. A 140 mm PLA dovetail rail is bolted to the gripper body along the closing axis, and the moving finger is printed in one piece with a dovetail carriage and a module-1 rack 110 mm long. A 50T module-1 PLA pinion (pitch radius 25 mm) is screwed to the STS3215 horn and meshes with the rack, so the finger travels 25 mm per servo radian. Over about 3.6 rad of servo travel the fingertips go from about 15 to 105 mm apart. The finger slides straight, so its face stays parallel to the fixed face and its tip stays level with the fixed tip at every opening. That removes both the R(1-cos q) rise and the 45 deg tilt that put the moving pad on the top face of the 85-96 mm low objects. A printed preload gib with M3 set screws takes up dovetail clearance. The existing pads module mounts on the carriage face at pad_angle 0.
idea.test: Simulator builder: a prismatic jaw variant whose travel is not limited by the 100 mm rod. Settings: rail length 140 mm, pinion_teeth 50, servo range -0.17..3.6 rad (opening about 15-105 mm), slide friction about 0.3 (PLA on PLA), tip offset +0 mm, face 0 deg with pads at pad_angle 0 and groove_mm about 2. Run all 21 groups, with System 1 also tuning a gripper torque limit.

iterations.notes: Diagnosis: all four failing groups fail the same way, moving_jaw_on_top_face, and they are the only objects at 85 mm or wider. The stock hinge's fingertip rises (+29 mm at 85 mm) and its face tilts (45 deg at 85 mm), and the opening stops at 91 mm, below sugar (92) and mustard (96). No pad value fixes it. Raising pad_angle to help the wide objects has twice cost potted_meat_can (57 mm), and thinning the TPU cost it too. No catalogue swap fixes it either: the parallelogram tip rises even more (+49 mm at 85 mm), the prismatic tops out at 58 mm, and the 12 V servos are over budget and don't address this failure. So this batch is an idea only. It is new because earlier prismatic ideas needed 3 x 150 mm steel rods that are not on the manifest. This one uses a printed dovetail rail instead and needs nothing to buy: $0, 0 days of lead time, about 258 machine minutes. Nothing would need buying. The main risks are round objects held between parallel faces and squeeze on light objects, which needs a servo torque limit.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face. This is the mechanism in all 8 failing tasks. On the revolute, the moving fingertip rises as R(1-cos q) with R = 81 mm. The brief gives +19 mm at 75 mm, +29 mm at 85 mm and about +33 mm at the 91 mm cap. The opening also stops at 91 mm, short of sugar (92 mm) and mustard (96 mm). So the moving pad lands on the top face of tuna (34 tall, contact at +16 of top +17), pudding (38 tall, +18 of +19) and sugar (45 tall, +22 of +23), and above the equator of mustard (+29 of +29).
proposals.principle: A finger can only hold an object's side if, at that object's opening, its tip reaches below the object's top (or below the equator for a round object) with clearance above the table. A finger swinging on a circle of radius L rises by L(1-cos θ), where θ is its angle from the lowest point of the circle. Putting that lowest point in the middle of the working widths, instead of at the closed stop, keeps |θ| small at both ends. Holding the face orientation fixed (a four-bar) keeps the contact normals horizontal and opposed.
proposals.hypothesis:
Centred-sweep parallelogram jaw. This is the catalogue four-bar at link_mm = 90, but the links are mounted on the servo horn at a phase offset so they are vertical, and the fingertip at its lowest, when the fingertips are 45 mm apart. The catalogue part is lowest at the closed stop. Fingertip x = 45 + 90 sin θ, rise = 90(1-cos θ):
- 17 mm (dice): θ = -18°, rise +4.4 mm
- 19 mm (marker, equator 9.5): rise +3.8 mm
- 34 mm: rise +0.7 mm
- 57 mm: rise +0.8 mm
- 75 mm: rise +5 mm
- 85 mm (tuna, top 34): rise +9.4 mm
- 90 mm (pudding, top 38): rise +12 mm
- 92 mm (sugar, top 45): rise +13 mm
- 96 to 100 mm (mustard, equator 29): rise +16 to +19 mm
Every tip sits well below the top or equator it must reach. The servo sweep needed is about -18° to +38°, roughly 1 rad, inside the four-bar's -0.17..1.55 rad. The opening is no longer capped at 91 mm. Squeeze is T/(L cos θ) = 18 to 23 N, about today's 20 N. With TPU (mu 0.9) against cardboard at 0.5, 2 mu N is about 18 N, against 5.0 N of weight for sugar. Mustard (plastic, mu 0.4) gets about 14 N against 4.2 N.
Why cheaper moves will not do:
- Pads params: 4 trials gained 1 group. pad_angle 30 and TPU 0.5 each lost potted_meat_can. Pad_angle moves the face's parallel opening and lowers the tip only about 0.5 mm per degree, and the opening tops out at 95 mm.
- Catalogue parallelogram at link 90: the tip rises +49 mm at 85 mm, because it is lowest at the closed stop. Iteration 2 gained nothing and lost 7 groups.
- Catalogue prismatic: the largest pinion (60T) reaches only 58 mm.
- servos_12v: refused at $68 and does not touch this mechanism (sugar needs 0.41 + 0.77 = 1.18 N*m < 1.62).
The fix is the link phase, which no catalogue part exposes.
risks: large_marker and dice: at 17 to 19 mm the tip rises +4 mm against a 9.5 mm equator or 17 mm top. That margin is smaller than today's +0 mm. It should still hold, because the faces are now exactly parallel instead of 9° off.

potted_meat_can and cup at 57 mm: the face becomes vertical instead of +19°, which changes where the contact lands. Iteration 3's pad_angle 30 showed the can is sensitive to this (it slipped under load), so this is the main risk. Squeeze stays about 18 N.

Small objects: if the links intrude near the object at the closed end, the iteration-2 force_limit losses (dice, wood_block_cube, flat_screwdriver, large_marker) could recur. The link geometry must clear the jaw's inside.
Round rollers (golf_ball, tennis_ball, apple, plum, lemon, strawberry): flat vertical faces with tips below the equator should hold as they do now with flat pads.

idea.name: centred-sweep parallelogram jaw (phase-offset four-bar)
idea.description: Two printed PLA links, each 90 mm between pivots, carry the moving finger as a parallelogram four-bar, so the finger face stays vertical, parallel to the fixed jaw, at every opening. The driving link is keyed to the gripper-servo horn at a 0.31 rad offset, and the mount's pivot sits further out. Together these make the links vertical (fingertip lowest) at a 45 mm opening rather than at closed. The finger then sweeps about ±35° around that lowest point. The tip stays within about +4 mm of the fixed tip for 17 to 75 mm objects, +9 to +13 mm at 85 to 92 mm, and about +16 mm at 96 mm. It opens past 100 mm, and the horn sweep is under 1 rad. Pivots run on four MR63 bearings with M3 shafts. The existing TPU pads mount on the finger at pad_angle 0 (vertical face). About 20 g of PLA is added at the wrist, roughly 0.03 N*m at the shoulder.
idea.test: Add a link-phase parameter to the simulator's parallelogram jaw: the fingertip opening at which the links are vertical (here 45 mm), with link_mm = 90. Pads go to pad_angle_deg = 0, keeping pad_tpu_mm = 2, reach 0, groove 0, lip 0. Then rerun all 21 objects, checking two things: that the links do not collide with small objects at the closed end (the iteration-2 force_limit at t = 0.02 s on the wood cube), and the tip height against each object's top or equator.

proposals.result: idea recorded, not tested: centred-sweep parallelogram jaw (phase-offset four-bar); it would need $3.60 from the manifest, 3 days, 100 machine min; within the budget left

iterations.notes:
I'm proposing a new part, not a trial. If built, it would open past 100 mm and keep the moving tip within +16 mm of the fixed one, against the sugar box's 45 mm top. That should fix all four failing objects: tuna fish can, pudding box, sugar box and mustard bottle. It cannot be tested yet: the simulator has no setting for where the links sit when vertical, so it gets recorded and costed but not tried.

**Why no catalogue part or setting fixes this.** All 8 failing tasks fail the same way: the moving pad lands on the top of the object instead of beside it.
- **Current hinged jaw:** the moving fingertip rises as the jaw opens (+29 mm at 85 mm). The jaw also opens to only 91 mm, so it cannot reach the sugar box (92 mm) or the mustard bottle (96 mm).
- **Pad settings:** four trials gained one object (gelatin box). Two other pad changes lost the potted meat can.
- **Catalogue four-bar jaw (parallelogram):** its lowest point is at the closed end, so the tip rises +49 mm at 85 mm. It gained nothing in iteration 2 and lost 7 objects.
- **Catalogue slide jaw (prismatic):** it opens at most 58 mm.
- **12 V servos:** refused at $68 against $40 left, and torque is not the problem anyway. The sugar box needs 1.18 N*m against the 1.62 N*m stall.

**The new part.** It is the catalogue four-bar at 90 mm links, with the links mounted at an offset angle so they are vertical at a 45 mm opening. Since the fingertip rises with the angle from vertical, this keeps the rise small at both ends:

| Opening | Tip height vs the fixed tip | Object (limit) |
|---|---|---|
| 17–19 mm | +4 mm | dice (17 mm top), marker (9.5 mm equator) |
| 85 mm | +9 mm | tuna fish can (34 mm top) |
| 92 mm | +13 mm | sugar box (45 mm top) |
| 96 mm | +16 mm | mustard bottle (29 mm equator) |

Squeeze stays at 18–23 N, close to today's 20 N.

**Cost:** four pivot bearings ($3.60, 3 days), about 20 g of PLA (about 100 machine minutes), plus screws already on hand. That is well within $40, 7 days and 591 minutes.

**What it could break:**
- **Potted meat can:** this is the main risk. It is sensitive to the face angle, and here the face goes vertical instead of 19° off.
- **Small objects:** the links could hit them at the closed end, as in iteration 2's early force-limit losses.

**To test it,** the simulator's four-bar jaw needs a new setting: the opening at which its links are vertical (45 mm here). With that added, I'd run this as a jaw swap with the pads set to 0°.

I submitted no settings or catalogue swap this round. Every one available has either already failed or is predicted to lose held objects without gaining any.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face, in all 8 failing tasks (pudding 90 mm, sugar 92 mm, mustard 96 mm, tuna 85 mm). The hinged moving fingertip rises as the jaw opens and its face tilts. The brief gives +19 mm and 35 deg at 75 mm, and +29 mm and 45 deg at 85 mm, with a 91 mm limit. The moving pad therefore comes down on the top face: 19-23 N pushing 83-88 deg down, at +16 to +29 mm from the centre against tops at +17 to +29. It never reaches the side. Mustard (96 mm) and sugar (92 mm) are also wider than the 91 mm maximum opening.
proposals.principle: A finger can hold a side only if its tip reaches below the object's top at that opening, and two contacts hold only if their normals are horizontal and opposed. A fingertip on a swinging joint rises by about R(1-cos q) and its face turns by q. To fix this at 85-96 mm, the finger must move in a straight horizontal line, keep its orientation, and travel more than 96 mm. A scissor (lazy-tongs) linkage does all three with only pivots: its output pin moves along the scissor axis, its end plate stays parallel, and the stroke is amplified by 2nL.
proposals.hypothesis:
No catalogue part or pad value can fix this, and the record shows it. Pad parameters were tried 4 times for 1 gain. Pad_angle 30 and thin TPU at 17 or 22 deg each lost potted_meat_can. The reach-15 pads lost 8-10 groups. A larger pad_angle lowers the tip (+14 mm at 85 mm with pad_angle 45), but the face is still 14 deg off and smaller objects get -21 deg faces.

The catalogue alternatives fail on their own numbers:
- Parallelogram, link 90: tip +49 mm at 85 mm. It lost 7 groups in iteration 2.
- Prismatic: at most 58 mm even at 60 teeth, because the stroke is pinion radius times about 1.9 rad.
- servos_12v: $68 against $40 left, and torque is not the mechanism. The arm needs only 0.41 + 0.15 x 5.14 = 1.18 N*m for the 514 g sugar box, against 1.62 N*m.

The recorded ideas are all rod- or rack-bound prismatic variants (which run into rod length) or swinging four-bars (which still rise). The scissor finger is neither. It needs no linear rods and adds stroke by linkage gain rather than pinion radius.

Design: one X-stage of two 60 mm PLA links (n=1, L=60). The servo horn drives one base arm and the other base pin rides in a slot. At the output, one pin is fixed to the finger carriage plate and one rides in a slot. Finger position x = 120 cos(theta). From theta = 82 deg (15 mm) to theta = 37 deg (96 mm), 45 deg of servo travel (0.79 rad) covers dice through mustard. That is inside the stock servo window of -0.17 to 1.20 rad.

Squeeze is servo torque over 0.12 sin(theta): about 13.6 N at 17 mm and 17-20 N at 85-96 mm. Grip estimates:
- sugar, mu 0.5: 2 x 0.5 x 17 = 17 N against 5.0 N of weight
- mustard, mu 0.4: 2 x 0.4 x 17 = 13.6 N against 4.2 N
- tuna, mu 0.35: 2 x 0.35 x 18 = 12.6 N against 1.7 N
- potted_meat_can at 57 mm (theta 62 deg): 15.3 N squeeze, giving 10.7 N against 3.6 N

The finger stays at constant height with a 0 deg face. The TPU pads should go to pad_angle 0, since the pads no longer need to offset hinge rotation. The pad tip can then sit 3 mm above the table for every object, below the 34 mm tuna top and the 38 mm pudding top. Added wrist mass is about 35 g, which keeps the shoulder near 1.23 N*m against 1.62 N*m stall.

I am not proposing another pads-params trial. Interpolating the brief, pad_angle 22-25 at TPU 2 gives about 39 deg and +26 mm at 85 mm. That gains nothing and is the region that loses potted_meat_can.
risks: dice / large_marker / wood_block_cube: squeeze drops from 20 N to about 13.6 N near full close. The 5-16 g objects need under 0.2 N of friction, so they should hold. The real risk is closing accuracy, because the scissor's gain is lowest near collapse.

potted_meat_can: depends on the face being vertical. Pad_angle 30 lost it (slipped_under_load) when the face approached parallel at 57 mm, so the TPU friction and squeeze have to be re-tuned by System 1.

Round objects (apple, golf_ball, tennis_ball, lemon, plum, strawberry, racquetball): with vertical faces the contacts sit at the equator only if the pad height matches. Pad height now stays constant instead of varying with opening, so System 1 has to re-tune the grasp height.
Slot-pin play in PLA lets the finger tilt a little under load. M3 pins in MR63 bearings limit this.

idea.name: scissor (lazy-tongs) straight-line moving jaw
idea.description:
A single-stage printed scissor linkage (two 60 mm PLA link pairs crossed at their middles) replaces the hinged moving jaw. At the servo end, one link end is pinned to the gripper servo horn and the other slides in a printed slot. At the output end, one link end is pinned to a finger carriage plate and the other slides in a slot on that plate, so the plate translates along the closing axis without turning or rising.

The finger opening is x = 120 cos(theta). Over theta 82 to 37 deg (0.79 rad of servo travel, inside the stock window) the opening runs 15 to 96 mm, with squeeze tau/(0.12 sin theta), about 14-20 N. The TPU pad mounts on the carriage at pad_angle 0, so its face is parallel to the fixed jaw at every opening and its tip stays a few mm above the table for every object width. The fixed jaw is unchanged.
idea.test: A jaw builder for a scissor finger: a prismatic joint along the closing axis with a nonlinear transmission from the servo angle q (x = 2nL cos(theta0 - q), force = tau / (2nL sin theta)). Parameters: link_mm [40, 70] and stages n in {1, 2}. Face orientation is fixed at 0 deg and fingertip height is constant. Add slot-pin compliance of about 0.3 mm as a small rotational play on the carriage. Then rerun all 21 groups with System 1 re-tuning the grasp.

proposals.result: idea recorded, not tested: scissor (lazy-tongs) straight-line moving jaw; it would need $5.40 from the manifest, 3 days, 158 machine min; within the budget left

iterations.notes: I'm proposing a new jaw design (an idea, so it is recorded and costed but not simulated) instead of another parameter or catalogue trial. Every option the catalogue offers has already been tried or fails on the brief's own numbers, so none can fix the moving jaw landing on the box tops. The scissor jaw is built mostly from manifest parts. It costs $5.40 for 6 MR63 bearings with a 3-day lead time, plus about 160 machine minutes (30 g PLA and 1 g TPU), which fits in the $40, 7 days and 591 minutes left. No linear rods or racks are needed, unlike the six ideas already recorded, which all hit the rod length or still rise as they swing. To test it, the simulator needs a jaw builder for a nonlinear prismatic finger. If the run must use a simulated trial this iteration, no catalogue swap and no pad value is predicted to gain any of the four failing groups without losing potted_meat_can.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face, with a parameter trade-off behind it. A fixed pad on the hinge is parallel at one opening only: the face sweeps from about 9 deg swung in at 17 mm to 45 deg swung out at 85 mm. So any pad_angle that turns the wide-object face back (tuna, pudding, sugar) tilts the small-object and potted_meat_can faces past what friction holds.
proposals.principle: Antipodal contact at every opening needs a face that keeps its orientation against the object rather than against the jaw. A passively pivoting pad aligns to the object's side, because the contact moments about its pivot even out, so the normal stays horizontal whatever the jaw angle.
proposals.hypothesis: Six pad trials gained one group in total. Each pad_angle value either keeps potted_meat_can and the small objects or reaches the wide boxes, never both. A low-pivot self-aligning pad removes the angle trade-off: its bottom swings inward under the pivot at wide openings, so first contact falls below the object's top. It needs nothing bought, so unlike the iteration-5 swivel pad it has no cost and no lead time. It cannot reach mustard_bottle (96 mm > 91 mm opening).
risks: potted_meat_can: a compliant pad could let the heavy can rock about the flexure under lift acceleration

idea.name: TPU living-hinge self-aligning pad (manifest-only)
idea.description: A PLA pad plate is joined to a PLA base screwed onto the moving jaw by a 1.2 mm TPU flexure strip at the pad's lower third. The flexure axis is horizontal, along the jaw width. Its rest angle is 20 deg and it can rotate passively by about ±35 deg, with soft centring stiffness. When the pad meets an object's side, the contact moments about the flexure even out and turn the plate flat against the side, so the normal stays horizontal and opposed to the fixed jaw at any opening from 17 to 91 mm. Because the pivot is low, the plate's bottom swings in at wide openings and meets the side below the top.
idea.test: The simulator would need a pads variant whose moving face is a separate body on a hinge joint (spring stiffness about 0.05 N*m/rad, damping, limits ±35 deg) at a set height above the fingertip. It should be run on all 21 objects, with tuna, pudding and sugar as the targets and potted_meat_can and dice as the guard cases.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face. On pudding (90 mm wide, 38 tall), sugar (92 mm, 45 tall) and tuna (85 mm, 34 tall), the moving pad comes to rest on the top face, 85-88 deg down at +16 to +22 mm (tops at +17 to +23). Meanwhile the fixed jaw carries 0-10 N. At these widths the servo is near its 1.20 rad stop (91 mm maximum), and the moving face leans 45-50 deg with its bottom swung out (brief: 85 mm gives +45 deg). So the face above the fingertip leans inward over the box edge, and the pad lands on the top instead of passing down the side.
proposals.principle: A finger holds an object's side only if, at that opening, it reaches below the top with clearance. A tip contact on a vertical box or can side has a horizontal normal, which makes the grasp antipodal even when the pad face is tilted. A pad that extends past a swinging fingertip goes down along the jaw axis. At a jaw angle q, that moves the tip outward by about reach·sin q but up, relative to the fixed tip, by only about reach·(1-cos q).
proposals.hypothesis: Change only reach, from 0 to 6 mm. Pad_angle 17, 2 mm TPU, groove, lip and width stay the same. Every pad_angle and TPU trial so far (6 trials, 1 gain) rotated or thinned the face, and that moved potted_meat_can off its working geometry. Reach is the one pad parameter never tried at a modest value; only reach 15 was tried, in iteration 1. Near q ≈ 1.1-1.2 rad (sin ≈ 0.9, 1-cos ≈ 0.6), 6 mm of reach adds about 5.5 mm to the tip opening (about 91 to 96 mm) and raises the moving tip only about 3 mm against the fixed one. The face at a given height above the tip then sits about 0.84r + 0.46r·tan50 ≈ 1.4r ≈ 8 mm further out. On pudding the box top is about 3 mm above the moving tip during descent, so the inward lean there is about 4 mm, and the pad clears the edge (about 96 mm against 90). As the jaw closes, the tip comes down the side and presses its edge against the vertical wall. The longer lever (81 mm → 87 mm) drops the squeeze from about 20 to 18.5 N. With mu 0.5 that gives 2·0.5·18.5 = 18.5 N against 5.0 N for sugar's weight. The shoulder load is 0.41 + 0.15·5.14 = 1.18 N·m, below the 1.62 N·m stall. A catalogue swap cannot do this. Prismatic tops out at 58 mm. Parallelogram link 90 raises the tip +49 mm at 85 mm and lost 7 groups. servos_12v is refused ($68 against $40 left).
risks: potted_meat_can (57 mm, 370 g, mu 0.35): the most sensitive held group. Its contact point moves about 6 mm lower and 3.5 mm outward along the same +18 deg face. The face angle is unchanged, and that angle is what the pad_angle/TPU trials disturbed, so it should keep holding after System 1 retunes the close.

dice / large_marker / wood_block_cube: at 0.14-0.24 rad the extension moves the tip inward by under 1.5 mm, and 6 mm is well short of the reach-15 pads, which probably interfered pad-on-pad at the closed stop.
banana (70 mm, 38 tall): its contact moves lower and outward. Its fixed_jaw_missed failures came from the pad_angle 38/45 trials, not from reach.

I'm proposing two settings of the one pad parameter that hasn't really been tried: reach 6 mm and reach 10 mm. Both are pad changes only, at no extra cost: about 3 g of PLA and 1 g of TPU (about 23 machine minutes), and the M2 screws are reused. Nothing needs buying. **Why reach should help.** Extending the pads past the fingertip pushes the moving tip outward much more than it raises it. That widens the gap at the box's top edge by about 1.4 mm per mm of reach, so the pad can pass down the side. There it grips the vertical wall with its tip edge, which presses straight across and holds.

**Expected gains and risks.**
- I expect pudding, sugar and tuna to start passing; reach 10 might also clear mustard.
- The main risk is potted_meat_can, whose contact point moves lower on the pad. Small objects are a lesser risk: near the closed position the moving pad's bottom swings slightly inward.
- Reach 6 is the safer setting. Reach 10 has more margin for the wide objects but sits closer to the reach 15 that broke 8 to 10 groups in iteration 1.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face. All four failing objects (tuna 85 mm, pudding 90, sugar 92, mustard 96) are wide and low. On the hinge the moving fingertip rises as the jaw opens: +29 mm at 85 mm with the face 45 deg off parallel, and the opening tops out at 91 mm. So the moving pad comes down on the top edge. The trials show 19 to 23 N on the pad at +16 to +29 mm from the centre, where the top is at +17 to +29, pushing 83 to 88 deg down. Mustard (96 mm) does not fit inside the opening at all.
proposals.principle: A finger that translates along the closing axis neither turns nor rises, so its face stays vertical and its tip stays at grasp height at every opening. The required opening runs from 17 mm to about 100 mm, which is about 83 mm of stroke. Splitting that stroke between two racks driven by one pinion doubles the travel per servo radian without lowering the pinion's mechanical advantage per rack below what is needed.
proposals.hypothesis: No catalogue part or pad value can fix this, and the numbers show it. Revolute: at 90 mm the servo sits near 1.17 rad, with the tip about +32 mm and the face about +50 deg. Even with reach 10 the contact band stays in the top 6 mm of a 38 mm pudding box at a tilt whose tangent (1.2) exceeds mu, and reach 6 and 10 both lost potted_meat_can. Parallelogram at link 90: tip +49 mm at 85 mm, worse than now, and 96 mm maximum. Prismatic at 60 teeth: 58 mm maximum, which loses every held object wider than 58 mm. 12 V servos are refused ($68 against $40). The design: a 60T module-1 pinion (30 mm pitch radius) on the gripper horn drives two racks on opposite sides. Each rack carriage carries one jaw on its own pair of 3x100 mm rods, the two pairs stacked one above the other, which avoids the 150 mm rods the iteration-4 version needed. Stroke per jaw is 30 mm/rad x 1.92 rad = 58 mm, so the opening runs from about 0 to 115 mm, covering mustard at 96 with 19 mm to spare. Squeeze per jaw is 1.62/(2 x 0.030) = 27 N, against today's 20 N. Sugar at 514 g needs 5.0 N plus margin, and 2 x 0.9 x 27 = 49 N. Tuna on metal (mu 0.35) gets 2 x 0.35 x 27 = 19 N against 1.7 N. Faces stay at 0 deg, so the contacts are antipodal on boxes, cans and the lying bottle. Arm check: 0.41 + 0.15 x 5.14 + about 0.08 for about 50 g of extra wrist mass = about 1.26 N*m, under the 1.62 N*m stall. Both jaws centre on the object, which suits the rolling objects.
risks: dice and large_marker (17 to 19 mm): pinion backlash at 30 mm radius is about 0.1 mm per jaw, which is acceptable, but the closed stop must reach 15 mm, so the printed racks need about 2 mm of overlap past the centre.

potted_meat_can and tomato_soup_can (heavy metal, mu 0.35): squeeze rises from 20 to 27 N with the faces truly vertical, which should hold them better than today, where the face is about +18 deg at 57 mm.
golf_ball, plum, apple (round): flat vertical faces do not centre a sphere on their own. The existing pad slot (TPU, groove_mm) would carry over onto the carriages to centre them.
wrist mass and length grow, so heavy objects at long reach use more of the shoulder's torque margin.

idea.name: twin-rack symmetric parallel gripper on stacked 3x100 rod pairs (manifest-only)
idea.description: A printed 60T module-1 pinion sits on the gripper servo horn. Two printed racks mesh with it at the top and bottom, so they move in opposite directions. Each rack belongs to a carriage that carries one jaw (the fixed jaw becomes a second moving jaw). Each carriage rides its own pair of 3x100 mm ground steel rods on two LM3UU bushings. The two rod pairs are stacked vertically in a printed housing, so the carriages pass each other without collision and each gets 58 mm of travel. Both fingers stay vertical and at constant height. The opening runs 0 to about 115 mm, at 27 N per jaw. The existing printed TPU pads mount on the carriage fingers with M2 screws.
idea.test: A builder for a 'twin_prismatic' jaw: two slide joints coupled at a 1:-1 gear ratio to the gripper servo through a pinion of radius teeth/2 mm, with fingers that keep their orientation, a range of 0 to 58 mm per side, and squeeze = torque/(2r). Run all 21 objects, with System 1 refitting side clearance and the close target.

proposals.principle: A finger can only hold an object's side if its tip reaches below the top. If the pad's extension grows with jaw angle as R(1-cos q), the tip stays level, and extension along a jaw tilted by q also adds e sin q of opening.
proposals.hypothesis: This is a cheaper, stock-preserving alternative to a new jaw. The pad rides in a printed dovetail slide along the moving jaw. A printed push-link pinned between the gripper body and the slider (two MR63 pivots) drives the slider out as the jaw opens. The geometry is chosen so the extension is near zero below 0.65 rad (where potted_meat_can, cube, dice and the screwdriver are held now, so they see no change) and rises to about 25 mm at 1.15 rad. At 90 mm the tip would come down from about +32 to about +7 mm, beside a box that is 38 mm tall. The extension along the tilted jaw adds about 23 mm of opening, giving a maximum near 110 mm, which covers mustard. The face angle is still +45 to +50 deg at those openings, so this only works together with the iteration-5 swivel pad. That is why it ranks below the twin-rack design.

idea.name: opening-compensated telescoping pad on the revolute jaw
idea.description: The moving pad sits on a printed dovetail slider along the moving jaw. A printed push-link from a pivot on the gripper body to the slider (MR63 bearings at both ends) pushes the pad down the jaw as the hinge opens, by about 81(1-cos(q-0.6)) mm above 0.6 rad. This keeps the fingertip level with the fixed one at wide openings and adds opening at the tip. The TPU skin is kept.
idea.test: A pad builder whose reach_mm is a function of jaw angle: reach(q) = max(0, 81(1 - cos(q - 0.6))), applied to the moving pad only. Run all 21 objects.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face. This shows up on all 8 failing tasks, which are four objects 85 to 96 mm across. On the revolute jaw the moving fingertip rises R(1-cos q) as the jaw opens and its face turns with the hinge. In the brief, at 85 mm the tip is +29 mm and the face is 45 deg off. The current maximum opening is 91 mm, which is below sugar (92) and mustard (96) and leaves pudding (90) with 0.5 mm per side. The failing traces agree: the moving pad lands at +16 to +29 mm against tops at +17 to +29 mm, pushing 83 to 88 deg down, and the fixed jaw has little or no contact.
proposals.principle: Two contacts hold an object only if their normals are horizontal and opposed and both sit below the object's top. A finger that slides straight along the closing axis neither turns nor rises. Its squeeze is servo torque over the effective pinion radius, so it is constant at every opening. A gear stage lets a small pinion give a long stroke without the 88 mm pinion that direct drive would need.
proposals.hypothesis:
No catalogue part or pad value can fix this, and the numbers show it.
- Revolute: the hinge stop at 1.20 rad caps the opening at 91 to 95 mm with the tip 14 to 29 mm high at 85 mm.
- Parallelogram at link_mm 90: opens to 96 mm, but the tip is +49 mm at 85 mm, above tuna's 34 mm height.
- Prismatic at pinion_teeth 60: tops out at 58 mm.
- Pads: 8 parameter trials gained only gelatin_box. Pad_angle 30, 38 and 45, thin TPU, and reach 6 and 10 each lost potted_meat_can, and pad_angle 38 and 45 also lost banana.
- 12 V servos: refused ($68 against $40 left), and they would not help anyway. Sugar needs 0.41 + 0.15*5.14 = 1.18 N*m, under the 1.62 N*m stall, so lift torque is not the failure.

A compound-geared prismatic jaw:
- Drive: a printed 48T module-1 gear on the servo horn (r 24 mm) drives a 16T gear (r 8). On the same idler shaft (an M3 screw in two MR63 bearings) a 28T pinion (r 14) drives the rack. That gives 24/8*14 = 42 mm of travel per servo radian, about 80 mm over the 1.92 rad servo range.
- Squeeze: about 1.62/0.042 = 38 N before losses, roughly 30 N in practice, against today's 20 N.
- Carriage: one LM3UU on each of two 3x100 rods, side by side, so the carriage is only 10 mm long and stroke is about 80 to 82 mm. Fingertip gap is 16 to 98 mm.
- Face: rotates with nothing and does not rise, so it is 0 deg off and the tip is +0 mm at every width, with pad_angle reset to 0.

What that gives each failing object:
- Tuna (85): 6 mm clearance per side; contacts at mid-height (17 mm) are horizontal; 2*0.35*30 = 21 N against 1.7 N of weight.
- Pudding (90): 4 mm per side.
- Sugar (92): 3 mm per side; 30 N against 5.0 N.
- Mustard (96): 1 mm per side, which is marginal. It lies on its side, so contacts below its 29 mm equator push it up into the opposed pad rather than out.

Bill of materials: lm3uu x2 ($2.40), steel_rod_3x100 x2 ($3.00), mr63 x2 ($1.80), m3_screw x8 (on hand), PLA about 35 g. Total $7.20, 3 days of lead time, about 175 machine minutes, all within budget.
risks: dice / large_marker / wood_block_cube (17-26 mm): need the closed gap at or below 16 mm. The rack end-stop must be set so the gap at -0.17 rad is about 14 mm. With no rise or tilt, these keep horizontal contacts.

potted_meat_can (57 mm, metal, 370 g): it has failed every time its face tilt changed. Here the face is exactly parallel and the squeeze grows from 20 to about 30 N, which removes the tilt that caused the earlier squeezed_down_out and slipped_under_load failures.

round objects (golf_ball, plum, lemon, racquetball, tennis_ball, apple, tomato_soup_can): flat parallel faces do not centre a sphere. Contacts must sit at the equator, which a non-rising tip makes easier than today. If needed, the pads' groove_mm (2-3 mm) can centre them.
all groups: adds about 40 g at the wrist. Worst case is sugar at about 1.24 N*m against 1.62 N*m stall, still about 25% margin.

idea.name: compound-geared long-stroke prismatic jaw (3x100 rods, 48T:16T + 28T pinion)
idea.description: The moving finger rides a carriage with one LM3UU bushing on each of two parallel 3x100 mm steel rods, so it slides straight along the closing axis without turning or rising. The servo horn carries a printed 48T module-1 gear. It drives a 16T gear on an idler shaft (an M3 screw in two MR63 bearings), and a 28T pinion on the same shaft drives a printed rack on the carriage. That gives 42 mm of finger travel per servo radian and a 16 to 98 mm gap over the -0.17..1.75 rad range. Squeeze is about 30 N, constant at every opening. Every gear stays 50 mm across or less, so the gripper stays compact; a direct 86T pinion would be 88 mm across.
idea.test: Add a prismatic-jaw variant to the simulator with a gear ratio parameter: effective radius = pinion_r * driver_r / driven_r, here 14*24/8 = 42 mm. Use the 82 mm stroke limit and a closed gap of 14 mm. Then run all 21 groups with pads pad_angle 0, TPU 2 mm.

proposals.result: idea recorded, not tested: compound-geared long-stroke prismatic jaw (3x100 rods, 48T:16T + 28T pinion); it would need $7.20 from the manifest, 3 days, 175 machine min; within the budget left

iterations.notes:
No catalogue part or pad setting can fix the four remaining objects, so I propose a new jaw part as an untested idea rather than a trial.

- **What fails:** pudding_box (90 mm), sugar_box (92), mustard_bottle (96) and tuna_fish_can (85) all fail the same way. The moving pad lands on the top face: the hinged jaw opens to at most 91 mm, and at wide openings its fingertip rises 14 to 29 mm and its face tilts up to 45 deg.
- **What has been tried:** 8 pad parameter trials gained only gelatin_box. Each one that moved the pad angle, thinned the rubber skin or extended the pads lost potted_meat_can; pad angles 38 and 45 also lost banana.
- **Catalogue jaws:** the four-bar opens to 96 mm but its tip is 49 mm high at 85 mm. The sliding jaw tops out at 58 mm. The 12 V servos are refused ($68 against $40 left), and the arm has torque to spare anyway.
- **The idea:** a sliding jaw driven through a gear stage. It gives 42 mm of finger travel per servo radian, a 16 to 98 mm gap, and a finger that neither tilts nor rises, with about 30 N of squeeze.
- **What to buy:** $7.20 of parts (2 bushings, 2 steel rods, 2 small bearings), 3 days of lead time and about 175 machine minutes, all within budget.
- **Overlap with the record:** it is close to the dovetail rack idea from iteration 8 and the twin-rack idea from iteration 13. The new part is the gear stage, which gets the full 85 to 96 mm range from rods on the bench without a pinion 88 mm across.
- **Risks to held groups:** the closed gap must be set to about 14 mm to keep the small objects (dice, marker, wood cube). Mustard_bottle is marginal, with 1 mm of clearance per side.
